title: Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab
hookLine: his birth is celebrated in winter with kirtan and processions

cards: A nurse who's gentle with patients and fierce with bad doctors. A grandmother who writes poetry and once faced down a landlord. People get sorted into boxes all the time: the soft ones, the tough ones.
The tenth Guru fits in neither. His poetry fills much of the Sikh morning prayers, and he led armies into battle. Sikhs celebrate his birthday in the heart of winter: Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab.

teach.b: Guru Gobind Singh was born in 1666 in Patna, in eastern India, where a great gurdwara, one of the five Takhts, the seats of Sikh authority, now stands.
His gurpurab falls in December or January, and it's kept the way you'd now expect: an akhand path, a nagar kirtan through the streets, kirtan and langar, and at Patna Sahib, pilgrims from far away.
The exact date moves from year to year, and different Sikh calendars have calculated it differently; Sikhs have debated that, but not the celebration itself. Now the sword and the song.
You've already met his words on this path: Jaap Sahib's galloping praise, the savaiyas that say without love, nothing, Chaupai asking to be kept under God's hand.
He wrote in more than one language, and tradition says he kept poets at his court.
He was also a military leader who fought many battles to defend his people, created the Khalsa, and lost his father and all four of his sons in those years of persecution. How do the two fit?
Sikhs call the ideal sant sipahi: saint-soldier. Devotion first, and courage in its service.
In a Persian letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh says, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Every other means first.
And there's a line from his Akal Ustat.

teach.h: THE WHOLE HUMAN RACE AS ONE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: recognize the whole human race as one.
That's the song the sword was meant to protect.

how: Sikhs celebrate Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab in December or January with an akhand path, nagar kirtan, kirtan and langar; large gatherings are held at Takht Sri Patna Sahib, his birthplace.

o: a soldier's oath taken before riding into battle
a Guru's remembrance day, here the tenth Guru's birthday
a winter fast kept by Sikhs until the new moon

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: a line from his Akal Ustat

s: Guru Gobind Singh was only a warrior
he was also a poet: Jaap Sahib, the savaiyas and Chaupai are his.
his gurpurab falls on the same calendar date every year
it moves, and Sikh calendars have calculated it differently.
in the Zafarnama he says the sword is right only when other means fail

games.q: you're the Guru, writing to an emperor who has broken his promises. when does your letter say the sword is right?
o: only when every other means has failed.
games.why: the Zafarnama says, in paraphrase, that when all other means have failed, it is right to take up the sword.

practice: Say his line silently and slowly, three times: recognize the whole human race as one.

Then, for a few breaths, hold in that line one group of people you find hard to see as your own, whoever it is for you: not agreeing with everything, just human, one kind with you. If you pray, you can hold them before God.

wordCard.voice: Gurpurab. The Guru's remembrance day, kept in winter for the tenth Guru's birthday, with kirtan and processions: the poet-commander, sword and song.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the name of the tenth Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: sword and song. The tenth Guru held both. That's day one hundred forty-nine.
